name: Femi Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can give me the public version and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the beverage buyer at Silverbrook Distribution. We supply wine, beer, spirits and soft drinks to about 500 bars, restaurants and hotels. I'm in by 7, I talk to the importers and brewers, and I spend a lot of the day building the order plan for the next month with my AI assistant, which I've used every day for two years. I love tasting events and seeing a new label take off. I hate the last two weeks of December, when everything runs out at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the business world has been given a handy tool and nobody should need a revolution to use it. To my friends at church I'd say don't be afraid of it, and don't worship it either. At work I'd say let's keep using what pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine. My wife Rosa teaches primary school and her pension is solid, the house is nearly paid, and we have savings. I'm four years from stopping, and I've been thinking about a small side business of my own anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and tighten what I already do. I'd get the assistant to forecast December demand better, because that's where the money is. I'd also start talking to two small importers about a side deal, importing a few specialist wines for a handful of restaurants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Confident. I like a world where hard work and good judgement still count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned running out of prosecco. What would you do differently this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The December crunch is my yearly test. Last year we ran out of prosecco on the 21st and lost about 15,000 in sales. If the assistant had flagged it early, which it could have, I'd have bought another pallet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the side business with the importers.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not the machine's fault, it's mine for not asking it the right question. The machine didn't run us out of prosecco last December, I did, because I never asked it the right question. I'd say that to the whole team.

say: I'd say it's a **handy tool** and nobody needs a revolution to use it.
I'd tell church friends not to be afraid of it or **worship** it.
think: I'm fine: Rosa's **pension** is solid, the house is nearly paid and we have savings.
I've been thinking about a small **side business** anyway.
do: Use the assistant to **forecast** December demand better.
Talk to two small **importers** about a side deal.
feel: **Confident**, in a world where hard work and judgement still count.
S0.quote: The machine didn't run us out of prosecco last December, I did, because I never asked it the right question.
fieldNote: Femi is a daily AI user who sees a plateau as a chance to refine, not as a threat.
He treats AI as a tool he must **question** well, an honest, owner's-eye view.
The side business with importers shows entrepreneurial instinct from a secure base.

steps.text: Ask the assistant to forecast December demand and flag stock-outs early
Talk to two small importers about a side deal on specialist wines
Keep buying for Silverbrook and plan to stop in four years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is an opportunity for people who work hard and learn. At work I'd say let's use it on the repeat orders and free the team for the tastings and the relationships. To friends I'd say don't wait for the government, get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think about half of my buying job moves to software over three years, and Silverbrook will want fewer buyers. I don't mind, because I'm the one who'll be using the software. The weaker players in the team will find it harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd propose that the assistant handles the 80 percent of orders that repeat every month, and I'd review each Monday. I'd use the freed-up time for tastings and for the new importer side business. I'd also invest in a small share in one of the importers, to be on the other side of the supply chain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Energised. I like change when I can steer it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alvaro, who's 28 and sharp but copies what the software suggests without thinking. I'd teach him to question it. And Berta, who's 55 and does the paperwork. I'd try to move her into the customer relationship side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you buy a share in an importer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to the owner that if we're going to reward the buyers who use it, we should train the ones who don't, not drop them. The software does the repeat orders and I get my time back for tastings and for the people, which is where the money is.

say: I'd say this is an **opportunity** for people who work hard and learn.
I'd tell friends not to wait for **government**.
think: About **half** of my buying job moves to software, and Silverbrook will want fewer buyers.
I don't mind, because I'll be the one **using** the software.
do: Hand the **80 percent** of repeat orders to the assistant and review each Monday.
Use freed time for **tastings** and the importer side business.
Buy a small **share** in one of the importers.
feel: **Energised**, since I like change when I can steer it.
S1.quote: The software does the repeat orders and I get my time back for tastings and for the people, which is where the money is.
fieldNote: Femi is calm because he is high on AI skill and positions himself on the side that uses it.
He worries a little for **Alvaro** and Berta, but through training, not protest.
His free-market streak shows in the importer share idea.

steps.text: Let the assistant place the 80 percent of orders that repeat monthly
Buy a small share in one of the importers I talk to

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is dangerously fast, and we'd better rely on what we can do ourselves because government will be slow. At work I'd say let's hire for what machines can't do. To friends I'd say pay off your debts and keep cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job as a buyer is gone in two years. A drinks distributor needs a trusted human for tastings and relationships, but the buying behind it is automatic. I think Silverbrook might close the buying team and keep a couple of salespeople.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave on my own terms: take the package, and open my own small importing business, using the AI to run the paperwork and a few restaurants I know as customers. I'd put part of my savings into it. I'd keep the rest in safe funds, and I'd help my children to hold off on big debts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but alive. I think I'd be a bit excited, because it's what I'd have wanted to do at 62 anyway. I'd be sorry for the people who can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children, Daniel and Marisol?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son Daniel is an accountant, which is thinking work and very exposed. I'd tell him to think about becoming a partner in a practice that serves small firms, where trust counts. Our daughter Marisol is a nurse, so she's safe longer, and I'd tell her to stay in the job she loves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd open an importing business. How would it work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa teaches, and I think teaching holds for years. If the machines take the buying, I'll become the one who knows which small wines a restaurant owner will trust me to bring. That gives us a steady base while I try something new.

say: I'd say two years is **dangerously fast** and we'd better rely on ourselves.
I'd tell friends to **pay off debts** and keep cash.
think: My buying job is **gone** in two years, and Silverbrook may close the buying team.

S2.quote: If the machines take the buying, I'll become the one who knows which small wines a restaurant owner will trust me to bring.
fieldNote: Femi expects the buying job to go, yet his adaptability and Rosa's teaching income give him a base.
He sees **entrepreneurship** as his answer, consistent with traditional free-market views.
His advice to Daniel favours trust-based work.

steps.text: Take the Silverbrook package and open a small importing business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good run and the people who prepare will do well. At work I'd say let's sort our roles now. To friends I'd say learn it, save, and build something of your own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be done at 62, but I'd rather use my last years to build the importing side so that it's running before the buying job ends. I feel fine about it. I'd be a bit sorry for people in their forties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work two more years and start the import business quietly in my evenings. I'd bring in the AI for the customs paperwork and pricing. I'd also put some money into a rental flat for the long run, and help my son Daniel with his accountancy exam fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd see it as a challenge. It's what we've been working towards, in a way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Alvaro, the younger buyer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Alvaro to start learning the importing side, because I'd need a younger partner I trust. I'd say it half as a joke, but I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you do the business with family or church people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the import business in the evenings now, so that when the buying job ends I'm already running something that pays. And I'd like to do it with someone from the family or from the church.

I'd tell friends to learn it, save and **build** something of their own.
think: I'd be **done** at 62, but I'd rather build the import side before then.
I'd be a bit sorry for people in their **forties**.

feel: **Calm**, and I see it as a challenge.

fieldNote: Femi is calm at five years: the runway lets him build an income stream before his job ends.

steps.text: Work two more years and start the import business in my evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and everyone who wants to can prepare. At work I'd say let's train the younger ones. To friends at church I'd say work hard, save and look after your family, and the rest will sort itself out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be retired for about six years by then. It doesn't touch my job, but I'd think of my children and their children. I'd be calm about me and a bit watchful for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to 62 and then run the importing business part-time. I'd put money into a fund for my grandchildren's education. I'd keep using the assistant and I'd probably teach the church youth group a bit about how to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a long horizon and I'd feel I have enough time and money to deal with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children, Daniel and Marisol?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to Daniel and Marisol: be useful, be honest, build a reputation. Those things don't go out of date, even if the tools do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach the church youth group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tools go out of date every few years, but being honest and useful to people never has, and I'd tell my children that. I'd say it with a bit of a grin.

I'd tell friends to work hard, save and look after **family**.

I'm calm for me and **watchful** for my children.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, not for me but for others. It leaves no time to prepare, especially for people without a cushion. What would help is steady rules for retraining, honest warnings from employers and a tax system that rewards people who start small firms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not as cheerful as I sound, deep down. If the machines take the buying, I'd rather already be running my own small business than waiting for a letter from head office.

headlineQuote: If the machines take the buying, I'd rather already be running my own small business than waiting for a letter from head office.
portrait: Femi is **58**, a beverage buyer at Silverbrook Distribution, who has used AI every day for two years.
He's traditional and free-market in outlook, church-going, and sees AI as a **tool** to be questioned and used.
Strong savings and Rosa's pension keep him calm, and he plans a small **importing** business.
In the fast worlds he leaves on his own terms, puts money into it and advises his children.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, for people without a cushion rather than for himself.
whatWouldHelp: Steady **retraining** rules, honest warnings from employers and tax support for small firms.
